meta.descriptionEn: In October 1927 the Italian liner Principessa Mafalda left Genoa for Buenos Aires carrying 971 passengers and 288 crew. The ship had already suffered breakdowns, spoiled food, failing water and a growing list. Then, off the coast of Brazil, a violent shudder ran through the hull. Rescue ships arrived within hours and the weather was clear, yet hundreds of people never reached safety. Why did a slow sinking turn into the worst loss of life in Italian shipping? Were the lifeboats ready? Who ignored the warning signs? This documentary follows the ship from her proud launch to her final night, and examines the investigation that followed.
meta.descriptionUr: Is documentary mein hum Italian jahaz Principessa Mafalda ki kahani sunate hain, jo 1927 mein Genoa se Buenos Aires ke liye rawana hua. Safar ke dauran hi jahaz mein kharabiyan zaahir hone lagi, khana kharab hua, pani ruk ruk kar aata tha aur jahaz ek taraf jhukne laga tha. Phir Brazil ke saahil ke qareeb ek zordaar jhatka laga. Madad qareeb thi, mausam saaf tha, phir bhi bohat si jaanen zaya hui. Aisa kyun hua? Lifeboats ka kya haal tha? Jaanne ke liye akhir tak dekhiye.

articleEn: At 22:03 on the night of 25 October 1927, an Italian ocean liner off the coast of Brazil lost all power and the whole ship was plunged into darkness. She was the Principessa Mafalda, carrying 1,252 passengers and crew, and until shortly before, everything had seemed under control. Just seven minutes later, at 22:10, the ship sank stern first, the rear of the vessel going under first. Before that, passengers had been jumping into the water.

Of the 1,252 people aboard, 314 lost their lives. It was the largest loss of life in Italian shipping history, and the ship came to be called the "Italian Titanic." Many details of that night are still disputed.

What is striking is that the ship sank about four hours and twenty minutes after the accident. Rescue ships had come close and the weather was clear. So how did a slowly sinking ship turn into such a huge tragedy? That is what this article tries to understand.

A second question is whether the lifeboats were really ready, and whether they could have been lowered in time and in the right way. Many of them are said to have been in poor condition. The third and hardest question is who was responsible. There is no one-sentence answer, because several conflicting versions of that night exist. To begin, we go back to the start of the story, when the ship was built and named after a princess.

articleEn: The ship's story began in the early twentieth century with an Italian shipping company, Navigazione Generale Italiana, known as NGI. In that era ocean liners were the main way to travel between continents, and they also carried mail and cargo. The route from Europe to South America was one of the big routes on which liners moved passengers and goods back and forth. Liners were built for hard open-sea conditions, so their hulls were often stronger than those of ordinary cruise ships. A liner is a ship that runs on a fixed route according to a timetable, and Mafalda was built for that kind of service.

For this route NGI had a new ship built and named her Principessa Mafalda, meaning Princess Mafalda. The name honored Princess Mafalda of Savoy, the second daughter of King Victor Emmanuel III, which tied the ship to the royal family. She was built at the Cantiere Navale di Riva Trigoso, where her sister ship, Principessa Jolanda, was being built at the same time.

Jolanda's story ended badly. On 22 September 1907 she capsized at her launch and sank immediately. This clearly affected Mafalda. To avoid repeating the disaster, a different method was used: on 22 October 1908 Mafalda was launched without her superstructure, meaning the heavy upper structure was added later. The ship was completed on 30 March 1909 and joined NGI's South American service that same year, becoming the company's flagship, its most prominent and prestigious vessel, the face of the fleet.

Consider the irony: a ship whose sister sank at launch became the pride of the company. Her job was the long voyage from Genoa to Buenos Aires, the route on which she would make her name over the coming years. She would later be called the "Italian Titanic," but in 1909 she was simply a new, splendid ship with a royal name. What lay ahead?

articleEn: Mafalda was designed specially for the Genoa to Buenos Aires run, and for many years she was regarded as the best ship on that route. Her speed was 18 knots, fairly fast for the time. A knot means one nautical mile per hour. Inside she was lavish, with a two-story ballroom and spacious cabins decorated in Louis XVI style. Passengers on liners of the era were divided into classes: cabin class was historically more comfortable, while steerage passengers stayed in large dormitories.

In 1910 the ship took on another role, when Guglielmo Marconi carried out long-distance radio communication experiments aboard her. This looks very significant in hindsight, because in October 1927 the ship's radio operators sent the SOS. Then came 22 August 1914. Shortly before the First World War, Mafalda made her only voyage from Genoa to New York City. South America remained her real field, and the New York trip happened just once before the war changed everything.

During the war the Italian Royal Navy requisitioned her, and she was used at Taranto as accommodation for officers. Many other liners in the First World War were turned into hospital ships or troop transports, so she was not alone. In 1918 she resumed her old South American service, and she remained NGI's flagship until 1922, when SS Giulio Cesare took over that position. She was no longer the company's most prominent ship, but she kept sailing. By 1926 she had completed more than 90 round trips, long but uneventful.

Once, it seemed it was all over. On 10 January 1920 news came that the ship was missing and that nobody had survived a collision with a mine. But only two days later Mafalda herself sent a radio signal saying she was perfectly safe and proceeding as usual. The report was false, and she carried on her normal voyages for years afterward. For roughly eighteen years she was tied to this route. Then came 1927. Was there any sign before that last voyage? We look at that next.

articleEn: On 11 October 1927 the Principessa Mafalda began her last voyage from Genoa to Buenos Aires under Captain Simone Gulì. She carried 971 passengers and 288 crew. Note that these add up to 1,259, while sources also give a total of 1,252. Aboard were 300 tonnes of cargo, 600 bags of mail and 250,000 gold lire for the Argentine government. The whole trip was to take 14 days, with stops planned at Barcelona, Dakar, Rio de Janeiro, Santos and Montevideo. On paper it looked like a long but orderly journey.

Soon it became clear the ship was in poor condition. Departure from Barcelona was delayed by about a day because of mechanical problems. Later, Mafalda stopped completely in open sea several times, sometimes for hours, leaving passengers waiting. According to sources, water in the bathrooms would come and go. Then the refrigeration system failed too. Tons of food spoiled and there were several cases of food poisoning. Imagine a ship stopping and starting in mid-ocean, short of water, with spoiled food. What were the passengers thinking?

Even so, the voyage continued. At Cape Verde the ship stopped, and Captain Gulì contacted the company, sending a telegram asking for a replacement vessel. The captain himself understood that conditions were not normal. The company's reply was brief: continue to Rio and await instructions. Instead of a replacement ship, he was ordered to carry on. The ship got fresh food and some repairs, but the repairs were only partial. In this state the captain took Mafalda into the open Atlantic. How many options he had, sources do not say; we only know the company told him to proceed.

Remember that by 1927 Mafalda was eighteen years old, having been completed in 1909 and made more than 90 round trips. The later investigation did not examine the questions of the ship's age and maintenance, which we will discuss in the final part. For now the picture is a tired ship, worried passengers and a company telling her to continue. Still, everyone was looking toward their destination. Buenos Aires was still far away, but something new had begun at sea. By 23 October passengers started to notice a small change. What was it? We look at that next.

articleEn: By 23 October the Principessa Mafalda had begun to lean to one side. The list was small but noticeable, toward the port side. Passengers had not been told much about the earlier failures, and now they began to worry that water might be filling the ship.

On 24 October the ship was running at full speed near the coast of northern Brazil. She was well behind schedule, but the mood had become calmer, with the longest part of the journey nearly done. On crossing the equator, a line-crossing ceremony was held on deck with orchestra music and a very large cake. Picture the music, the cake and smiling passengers. Then 25 October came, and everything changed. The ship had left on 11 October, and 14 days had now passed, the full planned length of the trip, yet she was still far from her destination.

At about 17:15 on 25 October the ship was near the Abrolhos Archipelago, about 130 kilometres out to sea from Salvador de Bahia. Suddenly she shook with several violent jolts, and people on deck panicked. Passengers were first told that a propeller had been lost and that the situation was not dangerous. That was a comfort, but the engineer's report on the bridge was different: the starboard propeller shaft had in fact broken, and had also shifted out of its axis. It cut several deep gashes into the hull. Matters worsened because the watertight doors, which are meant to hold back water, could not be fully closed.

About twenty minutes passed between the first jolt and the alarm. At 17:35 Captain Gulì sounded the alarm and ordered the radio officer to send an SOS, saying at the same time that it was only a precaution. He believed the ship could stay afloat until the next day. The SOS was answered quickly. Two ships, the British Empire Star and the Dutch Alhena, hurried to the scene. The weather was clear and help was close. On paper it should have been a successful rescue, and those aboard had hope: a wounded ship on one side, two rescue vessels and open sky on the other.

But in the next few hours the situation was about to change, as the ship's list and broken hull took their toll. Next we see how such a huge disaster happened despite help arriving, and where the sources disagree with one another.

articleEn: Now comes the hardest part of the story. The sources say plainly that several conflicting versions exist of what happened that night. According to some, the ship kept moving in a wide circle for at least an hour, which muddles the picture of the rescue. It is also said that the rescue vessels received confused signals about how to help, so communication was unclear. The rescue ships stayed at a distance, fearing a possible boiler explosion. Yet many of their lifeboats came near the sinking ship and kept transferring survivors, especially to Alhena.

The ship's own lifeboats were a problem. Because of the list, not all of them could be launched. Crowds rushed toward some boats, and several turned out to be unseaworthy through lack of maintenance, which became the root of later questions. Captain Gulì kept ordering the lifeboats lowered through a megaphone from the bridge. At first the evacuation was orderly. Then at 22:03 the ship's power failed, the whole vessel went dark, and panic spread quickly. Some passengers jumped into the sea. One account mentions sharks, but according to the sources such reports were never confirmed.

Gulì sensed the ship was now sinking fast and ordered all remaining lifeboats lowered. But the list to port made it hard to lower the starboard boats, and many struck the hull and became unusable. The situation on the port side was somewhat better, where First Officer Maresco was in charge. Still the problems continued. Many old, badly kept lifeboats began taking in water, and some were overturned by the weight of frightened passengers.

Stop and think: help was close and the weather was clear, yet one thing after another went wrong. That is why the story is so sad. Some accounts also include reports of suicides, which we will not detail because they are only reportedly stated. Accounts also say many first-class passengers stayed with the captain and did not bother to reach the lifeboats. The crowds, the darkness, the slanting deck and the faulty lifeboats together turned a slow sinking into chaos.

The ship went down about five hours after the first jolt, though the sources have their own time cues, one of them saying four hours and twenty minutes. What was the role of the captain and crew in all this confusion? Next we talk about those who did not leave their posts.

articleEn: Now to the rescue. The Principessa Mafalda sank in a busy shipping lane, so many vessels arrived to help. By daybreak Alhena, the Dutch ship that had arrived early on, had saved 450 survivors. Avelona then rescued 300 people. Empire Star, the British ship, took in 202. Formosa saved 151 and Rosetti 122. Moselle saved 49, of whom 22 were landed at Bahia. Behind every number were families.

The people rescued by Empire Star were later transferred to Formosa, and then landed at Rio de Janeiro. The disaster happened near the Abrolhos Archipelago, about 130 kilometres from Salvador de Bahia, and survivors were landed at Bahia and Rio de Janeiro. One curious thing: if you add up all these numbers, the total is greater than the 1,252 people aboard. Perhaps the Empire Star people were counted again on Formosa. That is only our guess, as the sources do not explain the difference.

Many reports about that night became famous. Gunfire, sharks, exploding boilers and nearby ships refusing to help were widely published. But the sources say plainly these were never confirmed, so we cannot present them as fact. There is another question: even today the exact location of the wreck is disputed, so not everyone agrees where the ship lies.

What was the significance of the disaster at the time? According to the sources, it was the largest loss of life on any Italian ship, and in the Southern Hemisphere as well. Of the 1,252 people, 314 died. The ship was in a busy lane, yet the loss was enormous. There is also a contradiction: two rescue ships arrived very quickly and the weather was clear, and still the chaos increased the toll.

So the real question remains: who was responsible? The ship's condition, the crew, the company, or something else? In the final part we look at the investigation's findings, the 2012 analysis, and the lessons of the disaster.

articleEn: Now the biggest question: who was to blame? The Italian Navy Board began its investigation right after the disaster. It concluded that the cause was a joint in the propeller casing, so a mechanical fault was blamed at root. The Board ordered that all Italian-registered vessels have devices fitted to their propeller shafts to protect against such accidents. This was a practical safety lesson: one ship's broken shaft created a new rule for the whole fleet. It was a heavy blow for Italian shipping of the time, since it was the worst loss of life in its history. The Board also found that six lifeboats at the stern could not be used because of poor placement.

But some things were not investigated. There was no inquiry into the ship's age, the lack of maintenance, or the actions of the crew. Recall that the ship had been traveling with continual faults, yet these questions did not appear in the official report. NGI was, however, ordered to pay heavy compensation to the victims' families, a way of acknowledging the loss financially.

Then came a 2012 analysis. According to it, the number of casualties among steerage passengers was indeed higher. But proportionally, 51.8% of first-class passengers died, while in steerage the rate was 27.8%. So the burden did not fall only on steerage passengers, and the numbers show a more complex picture. Another interesting finding: the survival rate for men was 74.1% and for women 73.3%, nearly equal.

What are the lessons? One, regular maintenance of ships must not exist only on paper. Two, the placement and readiness of lifeboats should be checked before every voyage. Three, clear signals and trained crew are essential in an emergency, since according to some sources the rescue ships received confusing signals.

Questions remain open: why a slow sinking became a disaster, whether the lifeboats were ready, and who was responsible. The answers we have are incomplete: a mechanical failure, faulty lifeboats and many conflicting accounts. Perhaps the whole truth will never come out. In the end, remember the 314 people who did not return from this voyage. Their story is easy to forget, but it is important to remember.

shorts.titleEn: The Ship That Kept Stopping at Sea: Principessa Mafalda
shorts.text: ایک ship جو سمندر کے بیچ بار بار رک جاتی تھی، پھر بھی اسے چلتے رہنے کا حکم ملا۔ یہ Principessa Mafalda تھی۔ 11 October 1927 کو وہ Genoa سے Buenos Aires کے لیے نکلی۔ اس پر 971 passengers اور 288 crew سوار تھے۔ ساتھ 600 bags mail اور Argentine government کے لیے 250,000 gold lire بھی تھے۔ Barcelona سے ship تقریباً ایک دن دیر سے نکلی۔ کئی بار وہ high seas پر مکمل طور پر رک گئی۔ refrigeration system خراب ہوا اور کھانا خراب ہو گیا۔ Cape Verde پر Captain Simone Gulì نے company سے نیا جہاز مانگا۔ جواب ملا: Continue to Rio اور instructions کا انتظار کریں۔ تو کیا ship آگے بڑھ پائی؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Ek ship jo samundar ke beech baar baar ruk jati thi, phir bhi use chalte rehne ka hukm mila. Yeh Principessa Mafalda thi. 11 October 1927 ko woh Genoa se Buenos Aires ke liye nikli. Is par 971 passengers aur 288 crew sawar thay. Sath 600 bags mail aur Argentine government ke liye 250,000 gold lire bhi thay. Barcelona se ship taqreeban ek din der se nikli. Kai baar woh high seas par mukammal tor par ruk gayi. refrigeration system kharab hua aur khana kharab ho gaya. Cape Verde par Captain Simone Gulì ne company se naya jahaz manga. Jawab mila: Continue to Rio aur instructions ka intezar karein. To kya ship aage barh pai? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
In October 1927 the Italian liner Principessa Mafalda developed mechanical problems after leaving Genoa, and at Cape Verde the captain was told to continue to Rio.
How did a slow breakdown turn into a tragedy?

shorts.titleEn: Music, Cake, Then Sudden Shudders: Principessa Mafalda's Last Day
shorts.text: ایک ship پر orchestra بج رہا تھا، اور پھر اچانک جھٹکے لگنے لگے۔ 23 October تک Principessa Mafalda port side کی طرف تھوڑی جھک چکی تھی۔ Equator پار کرنے پر deck پر ceremony ہوئی، orchestra تھا اور ایک بہت بڑا cake تھا۔ پھر 25 October 1927 کو تقریباً 17:15 پر Abrolhos Archipelago کے قریب کئی زوردار جھٹکے لگے۔ passengers کو بتایا گیا کہ propeller ٹوٹا ہے اور خطرہ نہیں۔ مگر bridge پر engineer نے بتایا کہ starboard propeller shaft ٹوٹ کر hull کو کاٹ چکا ہے۔ Watertight doors بھی پوری طرح بند نہیں ہو سکتے تھے۔ 17:35 پر Captain Gulì نے alarm بجایا اور SOS بھیجنے کا حکم دیا۔ کیا ship واقعی اگلے دن تک تیرتی رہتی؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Ek ship par orchestra baj raha tha, aur phir achanak jhatkay lagne lagay. 23 October tak Principessa Mafalda port side ki taraf thori jhuk chuki thi. Equator paar karne par deck par ceremony hui, orchestra tha aur ek bohat bara cake. Phir 25 October 1927 ko taqreeban 17:15 par Abrolhos Archipelago ke qareeb kai zordar jhatkay lagay. Passengers ko bataya gaya ke propeller toota hai aur khatra nahi. Magar bridge par engineer ne bataya ke starboard propeller shaft toot kar hull ko kaat chuka hai. Watertight doors bhi poori tarah band nahi ho sakte thay. 17:35 par Captain Gulì ne alarm bajaya aur SOS bhejne ka hukm diya. Kya ship waqai agle din tak tairti rehti? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
On 25 October 1927 a fractured propeller shaft shook the Principessa Mafalda off Brazil, and the SOS went out at 17:35.
What happened in the hours after the first shudder?

shorts.titleEn: Lights Out at 22:03: Who Stayed at Their Posts on Mafalda?
shorts.text: جب جہاز کی بجلی چلی گئی تو اندھیرے میں کون اپنی جگہ پر ڈٹا رہا؟ 25 October 1927 کو 22:03 پر Principessa Mafalda کی power ختم ہو گئی۔ Captain Simone Gulì bridge سے megaphone کے ذریعے lifeboats اتارنے کی ہدایت دے رہے تھے۔ جب انہیں اندازہ ہوا کہ ship تیزی سے ڈوب رہی ہے تو انہوں نے باقی تمام lifeboats اتارنے کا حکم دیا۔ ادھر دو radio operators، Luigi Reschia اور Francesco Boldracchi، آخر تک اپنی جگہ پر رہے۔ sources کے مطابق Captain Gulì ship کے ساتھ ہی چلے گئے۔ بعد میں تینوں کو سمندر میں بہادری پر posthumously اعزاز دیا گیا۔ 22:10 پر ship stern first ڈوب گئی۔ کیا اس رات کا ہر واقعہ واضح ہے؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Jab jahaz ki bijli chali gayi to andhere mein kaun apni jagah par date raha? 25 October 1927 ko 22:03 par Principessa Mafalda ki power khatam ho gayi. Captain Simone Gulì bridge se megaphone ke zariye lifeboats utarne ki hidayat de rahe thay. Jab unhein andaza hua ke ship tezi se doob rahi hai to unhon ne baqi tamam lifeboats utarne ka hukm diya. Udhar do radio operators, Luigi Reschia aur Francesco Boldracchi, aakhir tak apni jagah par rahe. Sources ke mutabiq Captain Gulì ship ke sath hi chale gaye. Baad mein teenon ko samundar mein bahaduri par posthumously aizaz diya gaya. 22:10 par ship stern first doob gayi. Kya is raat ka har waqia wazeh hai? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
After the power failed at 22:03, Captain Gulì stayed with the ship and two radio operators remained at their post to the end; all three were later honoured for bravery.
Many details of that night are still disputed.
